title: The Neutron and the Fundamental Particles Table
topicTitle: Discovery Of Neutron And Fundamental Particles
notes: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron and the complete subatomic-particle data table that the nuclear atom needs (electron, proton, neutron with charge, mass, discoverer and location).
### Why a third particle had to exist

Mass problem: helium (Z = 2) should weigh 2 protons ≈ 2 u, but weighs 4 u. Charge problem: nitrogen (A = 14, Z = 7) would need 7 electrons inside the nucleus under a proton-only model, making the atom's magnetism and the electron's confinement impossible (uncertainty: electrons cannot be confined to 10⁻¹⁵ m). A neutral, massive particle was required.

Polonium's α-particles hit beryllium and released a highly penetrating, neutral radiation: $^{9}\text{Be}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow\,^{12}\text{C}+^{1}\text{n}$. The radiation knocked protons out of paraffin wax; by conservation of momentum and energy the unknown particle's mass was calculated as ≈1.15–1.16 u — close to the proton's. Being neutral, it was unaffected by E/B fields and could pass through centimetres of lead.
• Electron (e⁻): charge −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (−1 unit), mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 0.000549 u = 1/1837 of H; discovered by J. J. Thomson (1897); location: revolving in orbitals outside the nucleus.
• Proton (p): +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (+1), 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00728 u; Goldstein's rays/identified by Thomson, named by Rutherford (1919–20); location: nucleus.

• Neutron (n): 0, 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00867 u (heaviest of the three); Chadwick (1932); location: nucleus. Free neutrons β-decay (half-life ≈ 11 min) because they are slightly heavier than a proton plus an electron.

Isotopes (same Z, different N), radioactivity (nuclear instability), nuclear stability (N/Z ratio ≈ 1 for light nuclei, rising to ≈1.5 for heavy), fission/fusion energy, and the notation ᴬZX that summarises every nuclide.
confusion: ❌ The neutron is lighter than the proton. ✅ It is heavier (1.675 vs 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) — hence free-neutron β-decay.
❌ The neutron was discovered before the proton was named. ✅ Proton named 1919–20; neutron 1932.
❌ Neutrons carry a small charge. ✅ Exactly zero charge; that is why they penetrate deeply and leave no ion tracks.

Neutron half-life outside the nucleus ≈ 10.7 min.
The neutron's magnetic moment is not zero (−1.91 nuclear magnetons) despite zero charge — evidence of internal quark structure.
examples: **Problem:** An atom has Z = 6 and A = 14. Give p, n, e and its isotope name. **Solution:** 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons — carbon-14 (¹⁴C), the dating isotope.

summary: A third particle had to exist. The mass problem: helium (Z = 2) should weigh 2 u if built from protons alone but weighs 4 u. The charge problem: nitrogen (A = 14, Z = 7) would need electrons inside the nucleus, which the uncertainty principle forbids, since confining an electron to 10⁻¹⁵ m demands ~10⁹ eV. Chadwick's 1932 experiment solved it: α-particles from polonium struck beryllium, ⁹Be + ⁴He → ¹²C + ¹n, releasing a highly penetrating neutral radiation that knocked protons out of paraffin wax; momentum conservation gave its mass as about 1.15 u. The complete table is: electron −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 0.000549 u, in orbitals, Thomson 1897; proton +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00728 u, in the nucleus, named by Rutherford; neutron 0, 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00867 u, in the nucleus, Chadwick 1932. The trio explains isotopes, radioactivity and nuclear stability.
importantConcepts: Why a third particle was needed: the mass problem (He = 4 u, not 2 u) and the charge problem (no electrons in the nucleus)
Chadwick's experiment: ⁹Be + ⁴He → ¹²C + ¹n, with protons recoiling from paraffin wax
Electron: −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 0.000549 u, outside the nucleus (Thomson, 1897)
Proton: +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00728 u, in the nucleus (named by Rutherford)
Neutron: charge 0, 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00867 u, in the nucleus (Chadwick, 1932)
importantStatements: The neutron is slightly heavier than a proton, so free neutrons β-decay with a half-life of about 10.7 minutes.
A neutral particle leaves no track in electric or magnetic fields and does not ionise gas, which is why it was missed for years.
The neutron's magnetic moment is not zero (−1.91 nuclear magnetons) despite its zero charge — evidence of internal quark structure.
A = Z + N, so a nuclide is written ᴬZX; isotopes differ only in N.
Stable nuclei need N/Z ≈ 1 for light elements, rising to about 1.5 for heavy ones.

keyPoints: The full table (charge, mass, discoverer, location) is a guaranteed short question.
Use the uncertainty principle — an electron cannot be confined to 10⁻¹⁵ m — as the conceptual argument for the neutron.
For any nuclide: protons = Z, electrons = Z (neutral atom), neutrons = A − Z.
The neutron's discovery made the fission chain reaction conceivable and led to the 1935 Nobel Prize.
specialNotes: The unknown radiation was first mistaken for γ-rays because it was neutral and highly penetrating.
Chadwick found a mass of about 1.15 u, slightly higher than the proton's — later refined to 1.00867 u.
The neutron is the heaviest of the three particles, yet carries no charge.
examShortTricks: Memorise all four table columns; short questions on the particles are guaranteed.
Both nuclear equations are worth quoting: ⁹Be + ⁴He → ¹²C + ¹n and ¹⁴N + ⁴He → ¹⁷O + ¹p.
For isotope questions, protons = Z and neutrons = A − Z, always.
